facts.statement: Camarasaurus lived during the Late Jurassic, from the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian ages, between 155 and 143 million years ago.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Jurassic, Kimmeridgian to Tithonian, 155–143 Ma

facts.statement: The genus Camarasaurus was described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1877.
facts.quote: authority: Cope, 1877

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Camarasaurus is Camarasaurus supremus.
facts.quote: type_species: Camarasaurus supremus

facts.statement: Other recognized species of Camarasaurus include C. grandis, C. lentus, and C. lewisi.
facts.quote: subdivision: *Camarasaurus grandis (Marsh, 1877) Camarasaurus lentus (Marsh, 1889) Camarasaurus lewisi (Jensen, 1988)

facts.statement: Camarasaurus was a sauropod dinosaur that lived in North America during the Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus ( ) is a genus of sauropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian to Tithonian ages, ) in North America.

facts.statement: More than 530 specimens of Camarasaurus have been found in the Morrison Formation of the western United States.
facts.quote: Over 530 specimens have been found in rocks of the Morrison Formation in the western United States, including several nearly complete skeletons.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus was a bulky sauropod characterized by a proportionally wide rib cage.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus was a bulky sauropod with a proportionally wide rib cage.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus had a proportionally large and strong skull with powerful jaws capable of high bite forces.
facts.quote: Its skull was proportionally larger and more strongly built than that of other sauropods, with powerful jaws that allowed for high bite forces.

facts.statement: The teeth of Camarasaurus were spoon-shaped, tilted forward, and rapidly replaced.
facts.quote: The teeth were spoon-shaped, tilted forwards, and rapidly replaced.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus was likely a selective feeder that browsed at heights ranging from 2 to 5 meters.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus was probably a selective feeder that fed at heights of 2 to 5 m.

facts.statement: Some Camarasaurus specimens represent embryos, while others reached an estimated age of 40 years, making them among the oldest known individual dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Specimens range from a presumed embryo to an individual that probably reached 40 years of age, one of the oldest reported ages for an individual dinosaur.

facts.statement: Skin impressions have been preserved on one Camarasaurus specimen, and others show evidence of injuries like bite marks and arthritis.
facts.quote: Skin impressions have been found on one specimen, and several specimens show signs of injury or disease, such as bite marks and arthritis.

facts.statement: The genus Camarasaurus was named in 1877 by Edward Drinker Cope based on fossils discovered at Garden Park, Colorado.
facts.quote: The genus was named in 1877 by Edward Drinker Cope, based on fossils from Garden Park, Colorado.

facts.statement: A life-sized drawing of a reconstructed Camarasaurus skeleton, likely made in 1879, is the oldest known sauropod reconstruction.
facts.quote: Probably in 1879, a life-sized drawing of the reconstructed skeleton was made, the oldest known reconstruction of a sauropod.

facts.statement: Since 1909, several largely complete Camarasaurus skeletons have been found in the Carnegie Quarry at Dinosaur National Monument.
facts.quote: From 1909, several largely complete skeletons have been discovered in Carnegie Quarry at what is now Dinosaur National Monument

facts.statement: The species C. supremus was considerably larger than other Camarasaurus species.
facts.quote: C. supremus was considerably larger.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus is classified as a member of the sauropod group Macronaria.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus is a member of the group Macronaria.

facts.statement: Some paleontologists debate the classification of Camarasaurus, suggesting it belongs in the family Camarasauridae alongside genera like Tehuelchesaurus and Lourinhasaurus.
facts.quote: Some paleontologists have grouped Camarasaurus with genera like Tehuelchesaurus and Lourinhasaurus in the family Camarasauridae.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus was discovered during the 'Bone Wars', a rivalry between paleontologists Othniel Charles Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope that spurred fossil discoveries in the late 19th century.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus was discovered during the Bone Wars, a feud between two American paleontologists, Othniel Charles Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope, that led to a surge of fossil discoveries in the Western United States in the late 19th century.

facts.statement: Cope named the fossils Camarasaurus supremus in a publication written in 1877.
facts.quote: Cope gave these fossils the name Camarasaurus supremus in another quickly written 1877 publication.

facts.statement: Oramel W. Lucas and his brother Ira H. Lucas sent fossils to Cope until 1884, providing much of the material for C. supremus.
facts.quote: Lucas and his brother, Ira H. Lucas, continued to send fossils to Cope until 1884, together representing much of the skeleton of C. supremus.

facts.statement: Zoologist John A. Ryder likely created a life-sized linen drawing of the Camarasaurus skeleton in early 1879 under Cope's direction.
facts.quote: Probably in early 1879, zoologist John A. Ryder created a life-sized drawing of the reconstructed skeleton on sheets of linen under Cope's direction.

facts.statement: The 68-foot-long reconstruction drawing was based on known Camarasaurus bones and the reconstructed limbs of Marsh's Morosaurus grandis.
facts.quote: The drawing was 68 ft long and was based on known Camarasaurus bones, as well as the reconstructed limbs of Morosaurus grandis that Marsh had published a few months earlier.

facts.statement: Because little was known about the skull and most reptiles were assumed to be carnivorous, early reconstructions depicted Camarasaurus with a hypothetical skull bearing long, sharp teeth.
facts.quote: Little was known of the skull at the time, and since most extant reptiles are carnivorous, it was assumed that the same applied to Camarasaurus. Consequently, the hypothetical skull bore long, sharp teeth.

facts.statement: Fossil bones were found by William Harlow Reed on March 7, 1877, south of Como Station in Wyoming.
facts.quote: On March 7, 1877, at roughly the same time when Lucas began collecting Camarasaurus bones at Garden Park, the railway employee William Harlow Reed found fossil bones on a hill south of Como Station, Wyoming.

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh described the first shipment of bones, cataloged as YPM 1901, as the species Apatosaurus grandis in December 1877.
facts.quote: In December 1877, Marsh described the bones of the first shipment (later cataloged as YPM 1901) as a new species of his previously established genus Apatosaurus, A. grandis.

facts.statement: Mook formally synonymized the genera Morosaurus and Camarasaurus in 1914.
facts.quote: In 1914, Mook formally synonymized the two genera.

facts.statement: An American Museum of Natural History team led by Walter Granger and Peter Kaisen began excavations at Bone Cabin Quarry in 1898.
facts.quote: In 1898, an AMNH team led by Walter Granger and Peter Kaisen began working at Bone Cabin Quarry, a newly discovered locality just north of Como Bluff.

facts.statement: Earl Douglass discovered Carnegie Quarry in 1909, which is now part of Dinosaur National Monument near Jensen, Utah.
facts.quote: In 1909, Earl Douglass of the Carnegie Museum discovered Carnegie Quarry, in what is now Dinosaur National Monument near Jensen, Utah.

facts.statement: William Jacob Holland described the genus Uintasaurus in 1924 based on five cervical vertebrae, but it is now considered a synonym of Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: In 1924, Carnegie Museum's director William Jacob Holland described the new genus Uintasaurus (after Uintah County, Utah) based on five cervical vertebrae from Carnegie Quarry; this genus is now considered as a synonym of Camarasaurus.

facts.statement: The skull DINO 28 was discovered in 1955 at Carnegie Quarry along with a fragmentary skeleton.
facts.quote: In 1955, the skull DINO 28 was discovered together with a fragmentary skeleton in the Carnegie Quarry.

facts.statement: Museum mounts of Apatosaurus were corrected to reflect its actual skull after it was identified in 1975.
facts.quote: These mounts were corrected after the actual skull of Apatosaurus was identified in 1975.

facts.statement: James A. Jensen collected a two-thirds complete articulated skeleton without a skull, cataloged as BYU 9740, from the Uncompahgre Plateau in 1967.
facts.quote: In 1967, James A. Jensen collected an articulated skeleton (BYU 9740) from the Uncompahgre Plateau in western Colorado; this skeleton was two-thirds complete but without skull.

facts.statement: John Stanton McIntosh and colleagues determined in 1996 that Cathetosaurus lewisi is a species of Camarasaurus, a view supported by most later studies.
facts.quote: In 1996, John Stanton McIntosh and colleagues determined that Cathetosaurus lewisi was a distinct species of Camarasaurus, as its differences from other Camarasaurus species were not general enough to warrant a separate genus; this opinion was supported by most later studies.

facts.statement: A 65% complete skeleton of C. grandis was collected in 1992 near Bone Cabin Quarry by Jeffrie Parker and his team.
facts.quote: In 1992, a 65% complete skeleton of C. grandis was collected by the fossil hunter Jeffrie Parker and team from near Bone Cabin Quarry.

facts.statement: A well-preserved Camarasaurus specimen was found in 1992 at Howe-Stephens Quarry in Wyoming by a Swiss team from the Sauriermuseum Aathal.
facts.quote: Another well-preserved Camarasaurus specimen was found in 1992 at the Howe-Stephens Quarry in Wyoming by a Swiss collecting team of the Sauriermuseum Aathal.

facts.statement: An incomplete skull with skeleton, cataloged as GPDM 220, was described in 2017 from the Little Snowy Mountains of Montana.
facts.quote: In 2017, the hitherto northernmost specimen, an incomplete skull with skeleton (GPDM 220) from the Little Snowy Mountains of Montana, was described.

facts.statement: The name Morosaurus refers to the animal's small brain size relative to its body size.
facts.quote: The name Morosaurus comes from the Greek μωρός (moros stupid), in reference to its small brain size compared to its body size, and σαυρος (sauros lizard).

facts.statement: Marsh noted that the limbs were shorter and the vertebrae were more robust with smaller cavities compared to other known sauropods.
facts.quote: Marsh noted that the limbs were shorter, and that the vertebrae were more robust and had smaller cavities than those of other sauropod specimens known at the time.

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn implied in 1898 that several genera, including Apatosaurus and Brontosaurus, were synonyms of Cope's Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: In 1898, Henry Fairfield Osborn, who despised Marsh, even implied that the genera Atlantosaurus, Apatosaurus, Amphicoelias, and Brontosaurus were all synonyms of Cope's Camarasaurus, which would have priority as it was named first.

facts.statement: It was debated from 1901 whether Morosaurus and Camarasaurus were the same genus, leading to their formal synonymization in 1914.
facts.quote: From 1901, several papers suggested that Morosaurus and Camarasaurus might be the same genus, and in 1914, Mook formally synonymized the two genera.

facts.statement: There was a debate regarding whether Cathetosaurus lewisi warranted a separate genus, but most later studies supported its classification as a species of Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: In 1996, John Stanton McIntosh and colleagues determined that Cathetosaurus lewisi was a distinct species of Camarasaurus, as its differences from other Camarasaurus species were not general enough to warrant a separate genus; this opinion was supported by most later studies.

facts.statement: Compared to other sauropods, Camarasaurus was relatively bulky with a wide ribcage.
facts.quote: Compared to other sauropods, it was relatively bulky with a wide ribcage.

facts.statement: Like the contemporary Brachiosaurus, Camarasaurus had an enlarged external nostril resulting in an arched forehead.
facts.quote: As in the contemporary Brachiosaurus, the external naris (nostril) was enlarged, resulting in an arched forehead.

facts.statement: A 2004 review identified four unique anatomical features in the skull, including a forward-tilted lacrimal bone, a short quadrate bone, a quadratojugal bone contacting the squamosal, and an oblique groove on the lower jaw.
facts.quote: According to a 2004 review, the skull showed four autapomorphies (anatomical features not found in related genera): The lacrimal (the bone that formed the front margin of the orbit) was tilted forwards; the quadrate, a columnar bone at the rear of the skull, did not reach the infratemporal fenestra as its upwards-facing part was short; the quadratojugal bone, which formed the rear-bottom corner of the skull, reached upwards to make contact with the squamosal bone; and the side surface of the lower jaw had an oblique groove running from the surangular bone forwards and downwards to the lower margin of the dentary bone (the tooth-bearing bone of the lower jaw).

facts.statement: Specimens had four teeth in each premaxilla, 9 to 10 teeth in each maxilla, and 13 teeth in each lower jaw.
facts.quote: Specimens had four teeth in each premaxilla (the front bone of the upper jaw), 9 to 10 teeth in each maxilla (the main bone of the upper jaw), and 13 teeth in each lower jaw.

facts.statement: The vertebral column consisted of 12 cervical, 12 dorsal, and five sacral vertebrae.
facts.quote: The vertebral column consisted of 12 cervical (neck), 12 dorsal (back), and five sacral (hip) vertebrae.

facts.statement: The two specimens preserving a complete tail each have 53 caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: The two specimens that preserve a complete tail (CM 11338 and GMNH 101) each have 53 caudal vertebrae.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope described the genus Camarasaurus in 1877.
facts.quote: In 1877, Cope described Camarasaurus as a new genus of dinosaur

facts.statement: Since 1998, Camarasaurus has been classified as a basal member of the sauropod group Macronaria.
facts.quote: Since 1998, Camarasaurus is generally classified as a basal (early diverging) member of the sauropod group Macronaria

facts.statement: In 1997, Leonardo Salgado and colleagues proposed the name Camarasauromorpha to unite Camarasaurus and Titanosauriformes, though this classification has not been widely accepted.
facts.quote: In 1997, Leonardo Salgado and colleagues proposed the name Camarasauromorpha, which united Camarasaurus and Titanosauriformes

facts.statement: Camarasaurus supremus, named by Cope in 1877, is the type species of the genus.
facts.quote: C. supremus, named in 1877 by Cope, is the type species (the species the genus is based on)

facts.statement: Camarasaurus lewisi was originally described as the genus Cathetosaurus in 1988 before being reclassified as a species of Camarasaurus in 1996.
facts.quote: C. lewisi was originally described as a distinct genus, Cathetosaurus, in 1988, but reclassified as a species of Camarasaurus in 1996

facts.statement: Camarasaurus supremus primarily lived during the Tithonian stage at the top of the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: C. supremus would have primarily occurred during the Tithonian, at the very top of the Morrison Formation

facts.statement: In 1877, Cope believed that Camarasaurus was capable of and accustomed to moving on land.
facts.quote: In 1877, Cope was certain that Camarasaurus "was capable of and accustomed to progression on land"

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh interpreted sauropods, including Camarasaurus, as semiaquatic, a hypothesis that became widely accepted.
facts.quote: Marsh interpreted them as semiaquatic, and his hypothesis soon became widely accepted

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn speculated that Camarasaurus walked on the bottom of lakes to feed on water and land plants, leaving the water only for reproduction.
facts.quote: Osborn speculated that Camarasaurus could walk on the bottom of lakes and feed on both water and land plants using its flexible neck, and only left the water for reproduction

facts.statement: In the 1970s, paleontologists like Robert T. Bakker and Walter Coombs refuted the semiaquatic lifestyle hypothesis by showing the skeleton was not adapted for swimming.
facts.quote: The hypothesis of a semiaquatic lifestyle was refuted in the 1970s, when paleontologists such as Robert T. Bakker and Walter Coombs showed that the skeleton was not adapted for swimming

facts.statement: Camarasaurus was a herbivore that likely fed on vegetation at heights between 2 and 5 meters.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus was a herbivore that probably fed at moderate heights of 2 to 5 m.

facts.statement: A 1998 study by Anthony Fiorillo concluded that adult Camarasaurus ate coarser food than Diplodocus, based on microscopic pits and scratches on their teeth.
facts.quote: In 1998, Anthony Fiorillo concluded that adult Camarasaurus consumed coarser foods than the contemporary Diplodocus, as evidenced by microscopic pits and scratches on their teeth.

facts.statement: In 2011, John Whitlock argued that Camarasaurus was a selective feeder due to its round snout, unlike the bulk-feeding square-snouted diplodocids.
facts.quote: Based on this observation, John Whitlock argued in 2011 that the round-snouted Camarasaurus and Brachiosaurus were selective feeders whereas the square-snouted diplodocids and rebbachisaurids were bulk feeders.

facts.statement: The diet of adult Camarasaurus likely included leaves from conifers like Cheirolepidiaceae and ginkgos.
facts.quote: The diet of adult Camarasaurus might have consisted of the leaves of conifers, such as those of the extinct Cheirolepidiaceae, and ginkgos.

facts.statement: In 2016, Mark Hallett and Matt Wedel suggested that female araucarian cones and resins might have supplemented the diet of Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: In 2016, Mark Hallett and Matt Wedel suggested that female cones of araucarians as well as resins might have supplemented its diet.

facts.statement: A 2025 analysis of tooth calcium isotopes found that Camarasaurus had a more mixed, less specialized diet with more woody tissue than Camptosaurus and Diplodocus.
facts.quote: In a 2025 analysis of calcium isotope compositions of teeth, Norris and colleagues found that Camarasaurus had a more mixed and less specialized diet with a higher amount of woody tissues than Camptosaurus and Diplodocus.

facts.statement: A 2016 study estimated that Camarasaurus had a bite force almost four times stronger than that of Diplodocus.
facts.quote: A 2016 study by David Button and colleagues estimated that the bite force of Camarasaurus was almost four times higher than that of Diplodocus.

facts.statement: The bite force of Camarasaurus reached up to 1978 newtons at the back of its tooth row.
facts.quote: The bite force was highest in the posterior portion of the tooth row, where it is estimated to have reached up to 1978 newtons.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus replaced its teeth on average every 62 days, a rate determined by daily growth rings known as von Ebner lines.
facts.quote: A tooth was replaced after 62 days on average, as indicated by daily growth rings called von Ebner lines that are visible in thin sections.

facts.statement: A juvenile Camarasaurus fossil from Wyoming contained 14 polished quartz stones between 1 and 13 cm in diameter, identified as gastroliths.
facts.quote: A juvenile and heavily scavenged Camarasaurus specimen from Wyoming was found with 14 polished quartz stones that are between 1 and 13 cm in diameter and have been identified as gastroliths (stomach stones).

facts.statement: The exact posture of the Camarasaurus neck remains a subject of scientific controversy.
facts.quote: The probable neck posture has been the subject of controversy.

facts.statement: A 2007 study by Paul Sereno suggested that the head of Camarasaurus was habitually tilted down by about 15 degrees, based on inner ear anatomy.
facts.quote: In a 2007 study, Paul Sereno and colleagues suggested that the head of Camarasaurus was habitually inclined downwards by about 15°, based on the orientation of the semicircular canals in the inner ear, which housed the sense of balance.

facts.statement: Modern evidence from anatomy and trackways suggests that Camarasaurus held its entire tail off the ground.
facts.quote: Sauropods are now thought to have had held their entire tails clear off the ground, as indicated by anatomy and trackway evidence.

facts.statement: In 25% of Camarasaurus specimens, the foremost tail vertebrae were fused together, a condition caused by ossified tendons rather than direct bone fusion.
facts.quote: In a 1991 study, Rothschild and Berman noted that in 25% of Camarasaurus specimens, some of the foremost tail vertebrae were fused together.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested that the fusion of tail vertebrae in Camarasaurus might be a sexually dimorphic feature occurring only in males or only in females.
facts.quote: Rothschild and Berman suggested that the fusion was a sexually dimorphic feature that occurred only in the males or only in the females.

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that in males, the stiffened tail supported whip-lash motions used during fights with other males.
facts.quote: In males, it could have supported whip-lash motions with the tip of the tail during fights with other males.

facts.statement: A Camarasaurus embryo fossil measured 37 mm in bone length, suggesting a total body length of just over 1 meter and a body weight of 7.5 kg.
facts.quote: The bone is 37 mm in length, suggesting a skull length of about 70 mm, a body length of just over 1 m, and a body weight of 7.5 kg.

facts.statement: In 2013, researchers examined a large Camarasaurus individual weighing an estimated 14.3 tonnes to reconstruct its life history.
facts.quote: In 2013, Eva Maria Griebeler and colleagues examined thin sections of limb bones of a large Camarasaurus individual (CM 36664) with an estimated weight of 14.3 tonnes.

facts.statement: A large Camarasaurus individual was estimated to grow at a maximum rate of 1.5 tonnes per year, reach sexual maturity at about 21 years, and die at around 26 years.
facts.quote: This individual was estimated to have reached a maximum growth rate of 1.5 tonnes per year, sexual maturity at about 21 years, and death at around 26 years.

facts.statement: As of 2024, the Camarasaurus specimens GPDM 220 and "E.T." are among the oldest dinosaur individuals identified, despite being relatively small.
facts.quote: As of 2024, GPDM 220 and "E.T." are amongst the oldest dinosaur individuals identified, even though representing relatively small individuals.

facts.statement: In 2002, researchers used oxygen isotope thermometry to analyze bone apatite in a Camarasaurus specimen to estimate body temperatures.
facts.quote: In a 2002 study, William Showers and colleagues used oxygen isotope thermometry to analyze the bone apatite (the inorganic component of bone) of a Camarasaurus specimen.

facts.statement: In 2011, researchers analyzed the tooth enamel of Camarasaurus and Giraffatitan using clumped-isotope thermometry to estimate body temperatures.
facts.quote: In 2011, Robert Eagle and colleagues analyzed the tooth enamel of two sauropods, Camarasaurus and Giraffatitan, using clumped-isotope thermometry.

facts.statement: Researchers estimated the body temperatures of Camarasaurus to be between 36 and 38 degrees Celsius, comparable to those of modern mammals.
facts.quote: They estimated body temperatures of 36 - 38 C, comparable to those of modern mammals.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the small juvenile Camarasaurus specimen originally identified by Marsh as an embryo is indeed an embryo, as no evidence supports that specific claim.
facts.quote: Although a small juvenile, there is no evidence that this specimen is indeed an embryo as proposed by Marsh.

facts.statement: The discovery of small Camarasaurus embryos provided evidence for oviparity, casting doubt on the hypothesis proposed by Bakker in 1980 that sauropods were viviparous.
facts.quote: The small size of the embryo provided evidence that sauropods were oviparous (egg-laying), casting doubt on a hypothesis proposed by Bakker in 1980 that sauropods were viviparous and gave birth to relatively large young.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the small Camarasaurus specimen "E.T." belongs to the same species as larger individuals or represents a new, particularly small species.
facts.quote: According to Waskow and Sander, the small size of "E.T." suggests that it could have belonged to a new species that was particularly small.

facts.statement: It is unclear which of the robust or gracile morphs in Camarasaurus represents males and which represents females, despite suggestions that they reflect sexual differences.
facts.quote: Ikejiri argued that the two morphs reflect differences between the sexes, although it is unclear which morph represents male and which represents female individuals.

facts.statement: Large bite marks on Camarasaurus fossils likely indicate attacks by Torvosaurus or Allosaurus.
facts.quote: The bones of several specimens show bite marks; large examples in the type specimen of C. lewisi probably stem from Torvosaurus or Allosaurus.

facts.statement: In 1996, researchers identified pathologies in thirteen vertebrae of a complete Camarasaurus grandis tail.
facts.quote: In 1996, McIntosh and colleagues described pathologies in thirteen vertebrae of the complete tail of the C. grandis specimen GMNH-PV 101.

facts.statement: A Camarasaurus specimen showed spina bifida, the first reported case of this condition in dinosaurs.
facts.quote: In two of these vertebrae, the neural arch failed to completely develop, a defect known as spina bifida – the first reported example of this condition in dinosaurs.

facts.statement: At least five vertebrae in a Camarasaurus specimen exhibited osteoarthritis.
facts.quote: At least five vertebrae show bone outgrowths around the joints of the vertebral bodies, indicating osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease).

facts.statement: Five consecutive tail vertebrae in a Camarasaurus specimen were pathologically fused into one structure.
facts.quote: Five consecutive tail vertebrae (49 through 53) are pathologically fused into a single structure.

facts.statement: In 2002, researchers identified erosions in a Camarasaurus tail as the oldest fossil evidence for inflammatory arthritis.
facts.quote: In 2002, Rothschild and colleagues identified these as pathologies the oldest fossil evidence for inflammatory arthritis.

facts.statement: In 2001, researchers described a periostitis injury in a Camarasaurus grandis humerus that may have caused a limp.
facts.quote: In 2001, Lorrie McWhinney and colleagues described a periostitis, an injury of the periosteum (the outer layer of bones), in a humerus assigned to C. grandis.

facts.statement: In 2016, researchers described five different pathologies in the feet of a Camarasaurus individual nicknamed "E. T."
facts.quote: In 2016, Emanuel Tschopp and colleagues described five different types of pathologies in the bones of the fore- and hind feet of "E. T."

facts.statement: Bony overgrowths on the hind feet of a Camarasaurus may have resulted from excessive claw use during scratch-digging.
facts.quote: Bony shelves extending above the front articular surfaces of the phalanges of the hind feet were interpreted as enthesophytes caused by the insertion of tendons. These may have formed due to excessive use of the claws during life, possibly due to scratch-digging.

facts.statement: In 2026, researchers found that Camarasaurus finger anatomy made previously proposed walking postures impossible.
facts.quote: In 2026, Philip Senter found that the fingers of Camarasaurus had a limited range of motion and that none of these proposed postures would have been possible.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus lived during the Kimmeridgian and Tithonian ages of the Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus is known from rocks of the Morrison Formation dating to the Kimmeridgian and Tithonian ages ().

facts.statement: Camarasaurus fossils are found across western North America, from Montana to New Mexico, within the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: The Morrison Formation covers about 1.2 million km2 of western North America, and Camarasaurus is found across this range, from more than 100 localities as far north as Montana to as far south as New Mexico.

facts.statement: Over 530 specimens of Camarasaurus, including about 50 partial skeletons, have been discovered.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus is known from over 530 specimens, including isolated bones and about 50 partial skeletons.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus is the most common dinosaur in the Morrison Formation and one of the best-understood sauropods.
facts.quote: It is the most common dinosaur of the Morrison Formation and, due to its abundance, one of the best-understood sauropods.

facts.statement: A 2003 survey found 179 Camarasaurus specimens, more than any other sauropod genus in the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: In a 2003 survey of more than two hundred fossil localities, Foster reported 179 specimens of the genus, comparable to Apatosaurus (112) and Diplodocus (98), but far greater than Brachiosaurus (12), Haplocanthosaurus (12) and Barosaurus (13).

facts.statement: Five Camarasaurus specimens preserve all or nearly all of their neck vertebrae, which is rare for sauropods.
facts.quote: Even though complete necks are rarely found in sauropods, five specimens of Camarasaurus preserve all or nearly all of the cervical vertebrae.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus accounts for 44% of juvenile sauropod specimens found in the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: 44% of the sauropod specimens found in the Morrison Formation that are smaller than 50% of adult size are from Camarasaurus.

facts.statement: In 2011, researchers analyzed oxygen isotopes in Camarasaurus teeth to study its environment.
facts.quote: In 2011, Henry Fricke and colleagues analyzed the relative abundance of oxygen isotopes (δ18O, or delta-O-18, values) in both Camarasaurus teeth and carbonate rocks across the Morrison basin.

facts.statement: Large Camarasaurus individuals were likely immune from predation by theropods like Torvosaurus.
facts.quote: Large individuals of Camarasaurus would therefore have been largely immune from predation.

facts.statement: The genus Camarasaurus was named by Cope in 1877.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Cope, 1877

facts.statement: Camarasaurus grandis and Camarasaurus lentus are recognized species within the genus.
facts.quote: subdivision: Camarasaurus grandis (Marsh, 1877) Camarasaurus lentus (Marsh, 1889)

facts.statement: Caulodon, Morosaurus, and Uintasaurus are synonyms of the genus Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: synonyms: Caulodon Cope, 1877c Morosaurus Marsh, 1878 Uintasaurus Holland, 1924

facts.statement: Camarasaurus lived during the late Jurassic Period, approximately 155 to 145 million years ago, in the Kimmeridgian and Tithonian stages.
facts.quote: vivieron a finales del período Jurásico, hace aproximadamente 155 y 145 millones de años, en el Kimmeridgiense y el Titoniense

facts.statement: Fossils of Camarasaurus have been found in what is now North America and France.
facts.quote: en lo que hoy es Norteamérica y Francia

facts.statement: Camarasaurus was a quadrupedal herbivorous dinosaur.
facts.quote: Era un dinosaurio cuadrúpedo y herbívoro

facts.statement: Camarasaurus was the most abundant dinosaur species found in the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: los Camarasaurus son los más abundantes de todos los dinosaurios en la formación

facts.statement: The name Camarasaurus refers to the hollow spaces found in its vertebrae.
facts.quote: Su nombre se refiere a los huecos en las vértebras

facts.statement: Camarasaurus had much thicker bones than Diplodocus, making it heavier despite having air-filled chambers in its spine that reduced weight.
facts.quote: Los huesos de este gran herbívoro eran mucho más gruesos que los del Diplodocus, por lo que era más pesado a pesar de tener cámaras que reducían el peso de la columna vertebral

facts.statement: Camarasaurus likely could not stand on its hind legs because its thick bones and large front limbs made its front body too heavy to lift off the ground.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus probablemente no podía pararse en sus patas traseras ya que los huesos más gruesos y las grandes extremidades delanteras indicaban que la parte frontal del cuerpo era demasiado pesada para poder levantarla del suelo

facts.statement: The most common species, Camarasaurus lentus, reached a maximum length of about 15 meters.
facts.quote: El tamaño máximo de la especie más común, C. lentus, era de unos 15 metros de longitud

facts.statement: The largest species, Camarasaurus supremus, reached a maximum length of 23 meters and an estimated weight of 47 tons.
facts.quote: La especie más grande, C. supremus, alcanzó una longitud máxima de 23 metros y un peso máximo estimado de 47 toneladas

facts.statement: Camarasaurus had an arched, notably square skull with a blunt snout containing many fenestrae, though it was robust.
facts.quote: El cráneo arqueado de Camarasaurus era notablemente cuadrado y el hocico embotado tenía muchas fenestras, aunque era robusto

facts.statement: Camarasaurus had chisel-shaped teeth up to 19 centimeters long arranged uniformly along its jaw.
facts.quote: Los dientes de 19 centímetros de largo tenían forma de cinceles y estaban colocados uniformemente a lo largo de la quijada

facts.statement: The strength of its teeth suggests Camarasaurus likely ate tougher plant material than Diplodocus, which had thinner teeth.
facts.quote: La fuerza de los dientes indica que Camarasaurus comió probablemente un material vegetal más duro que los diplodócidos de dientes delgados

facts.statement: Camarasaurus lived in open conifer forests where hard-edible plants were abundant.
facts.quote: Vivía en bosques de coníferas abiertos donde se encontraban por doquier plantas alimenticias duras

facts.statement: It is debated whether Camarasaurus swallowed gastroliths to help grind food; recent analysis of stomach stone evidence suggests this was not the case.
facts.quote: Anteriormente, los científicos han sugerido que Camarasaurus y otros saurópodos pueden haber tragado gastrolitos, piedras, para ayudar a triturar los alimentos en el estómago, regurgitándolos cuando se volvían demasiado lisos. Un análisis más reciente, sin embargo, de la evidencia de las piedras del estómago sugiere que este no fue el caso

facts.statement: Camarasaurus had more developed strong, robust teeth than most sauropods, replaced every 62 days on average, indicating it could chew food to some degree before swallowing.
facts.quote: Los dientes fuertes y robustos de Camarasaurus estaban más desarrollados que los de la mayoría de los saurópodos y eran reemplazados en promedio cada 62 días, lo que indica que Camarasaurus pudo masticar los alimentos en su boca hasta cierto grado antes de tragar

facts.statement: Evidence suggests Camarasaurus preferred different vegetation than other sauropods, allowing them to share habitats without competition.
facts.quote: Otros hallazgos indican que Camarasaurus prefería vegetación diferente de la de otros saurópodos, Permitiéndoles compartir el mismo hábitat sin competir

facts.statement: Camarasaurus feet had five toes each, with the inner toe possessing a large, sharp claw for self-defense.
facts.quote: Los pies del Camarasaurus tenían cinco dedos cada uno, con el dedo del pie interno con una garra afilada grande para la autodefensa

facts.statement: Like modern elephants, Camarasaurus likely had a wedge of spongy tissue at the heel base to support its massive weight.
facts.quote: Como un elefante moderno, Camarasaurus parece haber tenido una cuña de tejido esponjoso en la base del talón, para apoyar el peso de una criatura tan grande

facts.statement: Camarasaurus had a shorter neck and tail than typically seen in sauropods of its size.
facts.quote: El cuello y la cola eran más cortos que lo que generalmente se ve en saurópodos de este tamaño

facts.statement: Camarasaurus vertebrae were filled with passages and cavities for an intricate system of air sacs connected to the lungs.
facts.quote: Las vértebras estaban plagadas de pasajes y cavidades para un intrincado sistema de sacos de aire conectados a los pulmones

facts.statement: The absence of upward projections on Camarasaurus vertebrae suggests it could not stand on its hind legs.
facts.quote: La ausencia de tales estructuras de la espina dorsal de Camarasaurus sugiere que no pudiera levantarse en sus patas traseras

facts.statement: Paleontologists originally believed the spinal enlargement was a second brain, but modern opinion suggests it was likely a large area of nervous reflex activity rather than a brain.
facts.quote: Los paleontólogos creyeron originalmente esto era un segundo cerebro, quizás necesario para coordinar a una criatura tan enorme. La opinión moderna afirma que, mientras que pudo haber sido un área de actividad refleja nerviosa grande, no un cerebro

facts.statement: Camarasaurus is a genus of three known species of sauropod dinosaurs belonging to the Camarasauridae family.
facts.quote: Camarasaurus (gr. "lagarto de cámaras") es un género con tres especies conocidas de dinosaurios saurópodos camarasáuridos

facts.statement: The three valid species of Camarasaurus are Camarasaurus supremus, Camarasaurus grandis, and Camarasaurus lentus.
facts.quote: Las tres consideradas válidas son Camarasaurus supremus, Camarasaurus grandis y Camarasaurus lentus

facts.statement: The first Camarasaurus fossils were found in Colorado, USA, where scattered vertebrae were located by Oramel W. Lucas.
facts.quote: Los primeros fósiles de Camarasaurus fueron hallados en Colorado, Estados Unidos, unas pocas vértebras dispersas fueron localizadas en Colorado, por Oramel W. Lucas.

facts.statement: The genus was named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1877.
facts.quote: Fue nombrado por Edward Drinker Cope rápidamente en 1877.

facts.statement: The first complete Camarasaurus skeleton in North America was found by Charles Gilmore in 1925.
facts.quote: No fue hasta 1925, el año en que Charles Gilmore encontró el primer esqueleto completo del Camarasaurus en Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Other species include C. grandis (1877), C. lentus (1889), and C. lewisi, originally described as the genus Cathetosaurus in 1988.
facts.quote: Otras especies descubiertas incluyen C. grandis, que significa gran lagarto de cámara, de 1877, C. lentus en 1889 y C. lewisi, originalmente descrito como un nuevo género Cathetosaurus, en 1988.

facts.statement: Camarasaurus lived from the Oxfordian to the Tithonian stages, between 161.5 and 143.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Oxfordian to Tithonian (161.5 to 143.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: A fossil record of two adults and a 12.2-meter-long juvenile found together in Wyoming was excavated by the University of Kansas and the Center for Biodiversity during field expeditions in 1997 and 1998.
facts.quote: Hay un registro fósil de dos adultos y de un joven de 12,2 metros de largo que murieron juntos en Wyoming, excavados por la división de paleontología vertebrada del Museo Historia Natural de la Universidad de Kansas y del Centro de la Biodiversidad, durante las expediciones de campo en 1997 y 1998.

facts.statement: A 2013 study by Griebeler et al. concluded that Camarasaurus sp. CM 36664 weighed 14,247 kilograms, reached sexual maturity at 20 years, and died at 26 years old.
facts.quote: Un estudio de Griebeler et al. de 2013 examinó los datos histológicos de huesos largos y concluyó que el Camarasaurus sp. CM 36664 pesó 14,247 kilogramos, alcanzó la madurez sexual a los 20 años y murió a la edad de 26 años.

facts.statement: Isotope thermometry on Camarasaurus tooth enamel by Eagle et al. yielded temperatures between 32.4 and 36.9 °C, comparable to modern mammals.
facts.quote: Eagle et al. Realizó una termometría de isótopo agrupado sobre el esmalte que cubre los dientes de varios saurópodos jurásicos, incluyendo Camarasaurus. Se obtuvieron temperaturas de entre 32,4 a 36,9 °C, que es comparable a la de los mamíferos modernos.

facts.statement: A Camarasaurus pelvis recovered from Dinosaur National Monument in Utah shows bite marks attributed to Allosaurus.
facts.quote: Una pelvis de Camarasaurus recuperada del Monumento nacional Dinosaurio en Utah muestra marcas atribuidas a Allosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2001, McWhinney, Carpenter, and Rothschild described a 25 by 18 cm wide juxtacortical lesion on a humerus resembling woven fibers.
facts.quote: En 2001, Lorie McWhinney, Kenneth Carpenter y Bruce Rothschild publicaron una descripción de una patología observada en el húmero. Se observó una lesión juxtacortical 25 por 18 cm de ancho hecha de hueso que se asemejaba a fibras tejidas.

facts.statement: A 2013 analysis re-separated the genera Camarasaurus and Cathetosaurus.
facts.quote: Un análisis de 2013 dividió a los dos géneros nuevamente.

facts.statement: Senter (2026) presented evidence of a limited range of motion in the fingers of Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: Evidence of limited range of motion of fingers of Camarasaurus and Stegosaurus is presented by Senter (2026).

facts.statement: Carpenter, Ikejiri, and Wilson (2026) studied the postcranial anatomy of two immature Camarasaurus lentus specimens from Dinosaur National Monument, interpreting them as sequential ontogenetic stages to reveal morphological variability.
facts.quote: Carpenter, Ikejiri & Wilson (2026) study the anatomy of postcranial skeleton of two immature specimens of Camarasaurus lentus from the strata of the Morrison Formation from Dinosaur National Monument (Utah, United States), interpreted as representing sequential stages in the ontogeny of the species and providing new information on its morphological variability.
